There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is a debtor but claims to be a creditor; the person who is a creditor but claims to be a debtor; the person who is neither a debtor nor a creditor; and the person who is both a debtor and a creditor. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is a debtor but claims to be a creditor? Here, bhikkhus, someone has not given a gift, yet he says: ‘I have given a gift. He has not performed meritorious deeds, yet he says: ‘I have performed meritorious deeds. He has not fulfilled his duties to his mother, yet he says: ‘I have fulfilled my duties to my mother. He has not fulfilled his duties to his father, yet he says: ‘I have fulfilled my duties to my father. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who is a debtor but claims to be a creditor. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is a creditor but claims to be a debtor? Here, bhikkhus, someone has given a gift, yet he says: ‘I have not given a gift. He has performed meritorious deeds, yet he says: ‘I have not performed meritorious deeds. He has fulfilled his duties to his mother, yet he says: ‘I have not fulfilled my duties to my mother. He has fulfilled his duties to his father, yet he says: ‘I have not fulfilled my duties to my father. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who is a creditor but claims to be a debtor. He has not performed meritorious deeds, yet he says: ‘I have not performed meritorious deeds. He has not fulfilled his duties to his mother, yet he says: ‘I have not fulfilled my duties to my mother. He has not fulfilled his duties to his father, yet he says: ‘I have not fulfilled my duties to my father. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who is neither a debtor nor a creditor. He has fulfilled his duties to his father, yet he says: ‘I have fulfilled my duties to my father. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who is both a debtor and a creditor. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “It is wonderful, Ānanda! For, Ānanda, it is by means of such a statement that the Tathāgata is to be remembered: ‘The Blessed One is a teacher who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of direct knowledge, for the sake of full understanding, for the sake of complete exhaustion, for the sake of relinquishment. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. For, Ānanda, it is by means of such a statement that the Tathāgata is to be remembered: ‘The Blessed One is a teacher who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of direct knowledge, for the sake of full understanding, for the sake of complete exhaustion, for the sake of relinquishment. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan had a brahmin wife named Dhanañjānī, who was full of faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
Then the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī, while serving food to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, stumbled and three times uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!”
“Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan said this to the brahmin lady Dhanañjānī:
“In this very way, this outcaste woman praises the praise of that shaveling ascetic, whoever he may be.”
"Now, you low-caste woman, I shall refute the doctrine of that teacher," he said.

"Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, who could refute the doctrine of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Nevertheless, Brahmin, go; having gone, you will find out."
Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, angry and displeased, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“What, having cut what, does one sleep in happiness?
What, having cut what, does one not grieve?
Of what single thing, indeed, ... [is it that]?”
“O Gotamas, you desire slaughter.
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps in peace;
having cut off anger, one does not grieve.”
O Brahmin, the Noble Ones praise the destruction of anger, which has poison for its root and sweetness for its tip.
"For having cut that, one does not grieve.
When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!"
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways."
“Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I receive the full ordination.
Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received the full ordination.
Not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Bhāradvāja, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,

in no long time realized for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; having attained it, he dwelt therein.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the Arahants.

1. The Chapter on Arahants:
The Discourse on Abuse.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
The brahmin Akkosaka Bhāradvāja heard:
"It is said that a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan has gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the ascetic Gotama.
Angered and displeased, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, [he addressed] the Blessed One with improper words.
He reviled and abused him with harsh words. When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the brahmin Akkosaka Bhāradvāja:
“What do you think, brahmin?
Do your friends, companions, kinsmen, blood relatives, and guests come to visit you?”
“Sometimes, Master Gotama, friends, colleagues, kinsmen, blood relations, and guests come to me.
“What do you think, brahmin? Do you provide them with hard food, soft food, or refreshments?
“Sometimes, Master Gotama, I provide them with hard food, soft food, or refreshments.”
“But if they do not accept it from you, Brahmin, to whom does it belong?
“If they do not accept it from me, Master Gotama, it belongs to us alone.
“In the same way, Brahmin, when you revile us who do not revile you, when you anger us who are not angry, when you quarrel with us who do not quarrel—we do not accept that from you.”
"It is yours alone, brahmin; it is yours alone, brahmin.
For whoever, brahmin, reviles one who reviles him, scolds one who scolds him, or quarrels with one who quarrels with him—he, brahmin, is said to 'partake together' and 'exchange'."
Therefore, we neither eat with you nor share anything with you.
This belongs to you alone, brahmin;
this belongs to you alone, brahmin.”
“The assembly, including the king, knows you, Master Gotama, thus:
‘The ascetic Gotama is an arahant.
And yet, Master Gotama, you still become angry.”
“How can there be anger for one who is free from anger,
who is self-controlled and lives in equanimity,
who is liberated through right knowledge?”
For one who is thus tranquil and poised, it is worse for him who,
being provoked to anger, returns that anger in kind.
By not retaliating against one who is angry,
one wins a battle difficult to win;
he acts for the benefit of both.
Both for oneself and for another;
he who, knowing another is provoked,
remains composed and mindful.
While both are seeking healing—
for themselves and for others—
people think, "He is a fool."
“Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma.
When this was said, the brahmin Akkosaka Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! … [as before] …”
“I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama, may I receive the full ordination.
Then the brahmin Akkosaka Bhāradvāja received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received the full ordination.
Not long after his full ordination, the venerable Akkosaka Bhāradvāja, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,

in no long time realized for himself through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He dwelt having personally realized it.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is nothing further of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And so the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the Arahants.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.3 (SN 7.3, SN 189, PTS [1st ed. SN i 163, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 350)*
1. The Chapter on Arahants:
The Discourse to Asurindaka On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
The brahmin Asurindakabhāradvāja heard:
“It is said that a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan has gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the ascetic Gotama.
Enraged and displeased, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, [he addressed] the Blessed One with uncivil words.
He reviled and abused him with harsh words.
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.
Then the brahmin Asurindakabhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“You are defeated, ascetic! You are defeated, ascetic!
“The fool indeed imagines victory when he speaks harsh words.”
Victory indeed belongs to that wise person who practices forbearance; by that very act,
his opponent is made worse off.
He who does not retaliate against one who is angry conquers a battle difficult to win— the battle against an angry person by remaining unangered.
One acts for the benefit of both oneself and another,
having recognized that the other is provoked to anger.
He who, being mindful, attains tranquility—
seeking the healing of both himself and another.
“Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma think that he is a fool.
When this was said, the brahmin Asurindakabhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … he directly realized it. And the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the arahants.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.4 (SN 7.4, SN 190, PTS [1st ed. SN i 164, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 351) 1. Arahantavagga Bilaṅgikasutta At Sāvatthī. “Monks, suppose there were a man who, having eaten a meal of choice rice accompanied by various curries, would vomit it up and then eat a meal of broken rice. He would think thus: ‘I have eaten a meal of choice rice accompanied by various curries; now I am eating a meal of broken rice. Monks, what do you think? Would that man eat the choice rice again? “No, venerable sir. “Monks, what do you think? Would that man eat the choice rice again after vomiting it up? “No, venerable sir. Why is that? Because, venerable sir, that choice rice is a superior food, while that broken rice is an inferior food. “So too, monks, for one who has attained arahantship, the defilements have been vomited up. It is impossible for those defilements to arise again in him. For what reason? Because, monks, that arahant has abandoned the defilements, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. “Just as, monks, a man might eat a meal of choice rice accompanied by various curries, and then vomit it up and eat a meal of broken rice. Suppose he were to think: ‘I have eaten a meal of choice rice accompanied by various curries; now I am eating a meal of broken rice. What do you think, monks? Would that man eat the choice rice again? “No, venerable sir. “Monks, what do you think? Would that man eat the choice rice again after vomiting it up? “No, venerable sir. Why is that? Because, venerable sir, that choice rice is a superior food, while that broken rice is an inferior food. “So too, monks, for one who has attained arahantship, the defilements have been vomited up. It is impossible for those defilements to arise again in him. For what reason? Because, monks, that arahant has abandoned the defilements, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
The brahmin Bilaṅgikabhāradvāja heard:
“It is said that a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan has gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the ascetic Gotama.”
Angry and displeased, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood silently to one side.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the brahmin Bilaṅgika Bhāradvāja, addressed the brahmin Bilaṅgika Bhāradvāja in verse:
“He who bears malice toward a man who is without malice...”
"To a pure person who is free from blemish,
that very evil returns,
like fine dust thrown against the wind."
When this was said, the brahmin Bilaṅgika Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! … [as before] … he has directly realized it.”
And so, the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the Arahants.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 7.5 (SN 7.5, SN 191, PTS [1st ed. SN i 164; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 352) 1. The Chapter on Arahants (*Arahantavagga*)
The Ahiṃsaka Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the brahmin Ahiṃsaka Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the brahmin Ahiṃsaka Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“I am a non-harmer, Master Gotama; I am a non-harmer, Master Gotama.
“May it be so, according to your name,” [the Blessed One replied].
You might indeed be one who practices non-violence; he who does not harm by body, speech, or mind.
“He indeed is non-harming who does not injure another.
When this was said, the brahmin Ahiṃsaka Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … he directly realized it. And the venerable Ahiṁsaka Bhāradvāja became one of the arahants.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.6 (SN 7.6, SN 192, PTS [1st ed. SN i 165, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 353) 1. Arahantavagga Jaṭāsutta (The Matted-Hair Ascetic) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*). What three? The matted-hair ascetic who is a worldling, bound by the fetters of birth, aging, and death; not free from suffering, from the fever of defilements, and not yet cooled, one who has still a future life ahead. The matted-hair ascetic who is a trainee (*sekha*), one who dwells with his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, one who possesses the seven factors of enlightenment, one who is on the path. The matted-hair ascetic who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of matted-hair ascetics. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, is one a matted-hair ascetic who is a worldling... a matted-hair ascetic who is a trainee... a matted-hair ascetic who is an arahant? “Here, bhikkhu, a matted-hair ascetic who is a worldling, bound by the fetters of birth, aging, and death... [as above]... Here, bhikkhu, a matted-hair ascetic who is a trainee dwells with his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness... [as above]... Here, bhikkhu, a matted-hair ascetic who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed... [as above]... is liberated through final knowledge. This, bhikkhu, is called a matted-hair ascetic who is an arahant. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, that bhikkhu addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has taught us the Dhamma in brief... [as above]... This is called a matted-hair ascetic who is an arahant. Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ānanda and told him all that had occurred. The Venerable Ānanda then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported everything to the Blessed One. “It is so, Ānanda! It is so, Ānanda! When a bhikkhu has been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by me with a talk on the Dhamma thus, if he does not attain the supreme goal of the holy life—the unsurpassed security from bondage—either in this very life or at the breaking up of the body, then he is one of two destinations: either the state of non-perception or the realm of the Aviha devas. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, for a long time this mind of mine has been developed, well-developed in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves: ‘We will develop the four foundations of mindfulness... [The Buddha then repeats the instruction on the development of each of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as previously described. “This, Ānanda, is called a matted-hair ascetic who is an arahant. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Venerable Ānanda’s words. Thus have I heard. [The rest of the sutta follows the structure of the previous one, with the same dialogue between the bhikkhu and the Buddha, and the subsequent report to Ānanda. The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the brahmin Jaṭābhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the brahmin Jaṭā Bhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Entangled within, entangled without,
this generation is entangled by its own entanglement.”
“Gautama, I ask you this:
who can unravel this tangle?
“A wise man, established in virtue...”
Cultivating both the mind and wisdom,
the ardent and discerning bhikkhu shall unravel this tangle.
Those for whom lust, hatred,
and ignorance have faded away—
the Arahants whose taints are destroyed—
For them, the tangles are disentangled,
wherein name-and-form cease without remainder.
“Repulsion and the perception of form—
therein this tangle is severed.
When this was said, Jaṭā Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… And the Venerable Bhāradvāja has become one of the arahants.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 7.7 (SN 7.7, SN 193, PTS [1st ed. SN i 165; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 354)
1. The Chapter on Arahants:
The Discourse on Pure States.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the brahmin Suddhikabhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the brahmin Suddhikabhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One with this verse:
“No brahmin whatsoever is purified in the world,
even one who is virtuous and practices austerities;
only one endowed with true knowledge and conduct [is purified].”
Thus one is purified, not another person.
Even though one mutters much idle chatter,
one does not become a brahmin by birth alone.
Antoka-sambhu is defiled,
relying upon hypocrisy;
he may be a khattiya, a brahmin, or a vessa.
A Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla, or a Pukkusa—
whosoever is one who has aroused energy, is resolute,
and is constantly firm in exertion.
“One attains supreme purity—
know this thus, O brahmin.
When this was said, the brahmin Suddhika Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … And the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the arahants.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.8 (SN 7.8, SN 194, PTS [1st ed. SN i 166, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 356)*
1. The Chapter on Arahants:
The Aggika Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, a brahmin named Aggikabhāradvāja had prepared milk-rice with ghee, thinking:
"I shall offer it into the fire; I shall attend to the sacred fire-sacrifice.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
While wandering for alms from house to house in Rājagaha, the Blessed One approached the residence of the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja; having approached, he stood to one side.
The brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing for alms, and seeing him, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Endowed with the three knowledges,
noble by birth, and learned in many things;
perfected in both knowledge and conduct— ”
One might eat soma or drink milk-rice;
yet even by much chanting and recitation,
one does not become a brahmin by birth alone.
Antoka-sambhu is defiled,
shrouded by hypocrisy;
he who knows his former abodes—
He beholds both heaven and the states of woe;
moreover, having reached the destruction of birth,
the sage is perfected through direct knowledge.
By means of these three knowledges,
a brahmin becomes "thrice-learned";
one who is perfected in both knowledge and conduct—
“May you eat the *soma* as a drink.
“Let the venerable Gotama eat;
you are a brahmin,” [he replied].
“Food sung to by verses is not for me to eat, O Brahmin;
this is not the Dhamma of those who see clearly.
The Buddhas reject food sung to by verses.”
When the Dhamma exists, O Brahmin, this is the way of life:
[to serve] another who is a perfected one, a great seer,
whose taints are exhausted, and whose remorse has been stilled.
“Serve him with food and drink;
for he is a field for one who seeks merit.
When this was said, the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … And the Venerable Aggikabhāradvāja became one of the arahants.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.9 (SN 7.9, SN 195, PTS [1st ed. SN i 167, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 358)*
1. The Chapter on Arahants:
The Sundarikā Sutta.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans on the bank of the river Sundarikā.
Now at that time, the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja was offering oblations and tending the sacred fire on the bank of the river Sundarikā.
Then, having offered the oblations and tended the sacred fire, the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja rose from his seat and looked all around in the four directions, thinking:
"Who might eat this remains of the sacrificial offering?"
The brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree with his head covered.
Having seen him, he took the remains of the sacrificial offering in his left hand and his water-pot in his right hand, and approached the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One uncovered his head at the sound of the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja’s footsteps.
Then the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja, thinking, "This worthy one is shaven-headed, this worthy one is a shaveling," desired to turn back right there.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja:
"For even some brahmins here are shaven-headed."
"What if I were to approach him and ask about his birth?
Then the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Of what birth are you, sir?"
“Do not ask about birth; ask about conduct.
For indeed, fire is born from wood.
Even one of low birth who is a sage and possesses fortitude—”
He is a noble steed, restrained by a sense of shame.
Tamed by truth, endowed with self-mastery,
he has reached the end of knowledge and lived the holy life.
“Whomever one has brought [as a guest], one should invite him;
he, at the proper time, offers the sacrifice to those worthy of offerings.
“Surely this has been well-offered and well-sacrificed by me.”
That I might see such a master of knowledge as you;
for by not seeing those like you,
other people consume the remainder of the sacrificial offerings.
“May the venerable Gotama eat;
you are a brahmin.
“What is sung to the accompaniment of verses is not fit for me to eat.”
This is not the Dhamma for those who see clearly, O Brahmin;
the Buddhas reject verses sung as praise.
When the Dhamma exists, O Brahmin, this is the proper way of life.
And with food and drink, serve the Great Sage who is complete, whose taints are exhausted, and whose remorse has been stilled.
"For that field is indeed for one who seeks merit.
"Then to whom, Master Gotama, shall I give this remains of the oblation?
"Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among the generation of recluses and brahmins, including gods and humans,"
“Brahmin, this remains of the sacrificial offering would be properly digested only by a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata among the generation consisting of devas and humans.
Therefore, Brahmin, you should either discard that remains of the sacrificial offering where there is no greenery, or cast it into water where there are no living beings.”
Then the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja threw that remains of the sacrificial offering into water devoid of living beings.
As soon as that remains of the offering was cast into the water, it hissed and sizzled, smoked and billowed.
It was just like an iron plowshare heated all day long, which, when thrown into water, hisses and sizzles, smokes and billows.
In the same way, that remaining portion of the oblation, when thrown into the water, hissed, sizzled, smoked, and emitted thick clouds of smoke.
Then the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja, stirred with awe and his hair standing on end, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood to one side.
As the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja was standing to one side, the Blessed One addressed him in verse:
“O Brahmin, do not imagine that purity comes from kindling wood externally;
for the wise say that purity is not attained by that means.”
O Brahmin, having abandoned the burning of wood from the outside,
I who desire external purity kindle the flame only within.
With a mind constantly aflame and ever-composed,
I, an arahant, lead the holy life.
For pride, O Brahmin, is a burden as heavy as a carrying-pole.
Anger is the smoke, falsehood is the ashes;
the tongue is the ladle, the heart is the place of light;
the self well-tamed is the light of a man.
The Dhamma is a lake, O Brahmin, with virtue as its bathing place;
it is undisturbed, praised by the virtuous, and esteemed by the wise.
Therein indeed do those who have attained true knowledge bathe.
Those whose limbs are not yet healed do not cross to the further shore.
Truth, Dhamma, self-restraint, and the holy life—
these, O Brahmin, constitute the attainment of Brahman for one who sits in the midst.
“Pay homage to those who have become upright;
such a person, I say, is one whose essence is the Dhamma.
When this was said, the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … And the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the arahants.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.10 (SN 7.10, SN 196, PTS [1st ed. SN i 170, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 365)*
1. The Chapter on Arahants:
The Discourse to Bahudhītarā.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan had lost fourteen oxen.
Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, searching for those oxen, approached that grove;
having approached, he saw the Blessed One sitting in that grove, having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect.

Having adjusted his body and established mindfulness before him, he saw [the Buddha] and approached where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Surely it cannot be that for this ascetic, ... [text truncated] ...”
Fourteen oxen were lost;
sixty cows are not seen today.
Because of this, this ascetic is happy.
Surely there are no evil ones in this ascetic’s sesame field—
neither those with one leaf nor those with two leaves.
Therefore this ascetic is happy.
Surely there are no mice in this ascetic’s empty storehouse.
They dance with excessive vigor;
therefore this ascetic is happy.
Surely it cannot be that for this ascetic—
The matting is seven months old,
covered with mushrooms;
therefore this ascetic is happy.
Surely this ascetic has not seven widowed daughters,
Nor sons who are one-eyed or two-eyed.
Therefore this ascetic is happy.
Surely no tawny freckles have struck him, this ascetic.
He awakens the sleeper with his foot;
therefore this ascetic is happy.
Surely for this ascetic there is no...
At dawn, creditors urge him on,
saying, "Give! Give!"—
it is for this reason that this ascetic is happy.
“Indeed, brahmin,
my oxen are not fourteen;
they have not been seen for sixty days.”
Therefore, O brahmin, I am happy.
For there are no evil [seeds] for me in the sesame field, O brahmin.
With one leaf and two leaves,
by that, O brahmin, I am happy. For it is not for my sake,
O brahmin, [that I seek them].
In an empty storehouse there are mice;
they dance with great exuberance,
and therefore, O brahmins, I am happy.
For my mat, O brahmin,
has not been spread for seven months;
it is covered with uprooted plants.
Therefore, O brahmin, I am happy.
For I have no widowed daughters, O brahmin.
I have one son and two sons;
therefore, O brahmin, I am happy.
For it is not for me, O brahmin, [to worry about them].
Piṅgalā was struck by Tilakā;
she woke me with her foot,
and because of that, O brahmins, I am happy.
For I have no creditors at dawn, O brahmin,
who urge me on, saying, "Give! Give!"
"Therefore, brahmin, I am happy.
When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan said to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!"
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways."
"I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I receive full ordination.
Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.
Not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Bhāradvāja, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,

soon realized for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; having attained it, he dwelt therein.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is nothing further of this state”—thus he directly knew.
And the venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on Arahants.
Its summary verse: Dhanañjānī, Akkosaka,
Asurinda, and Bilangika.
Ahiṃsaka, Jaṭā, Suddhika, Aggika,
and Sundarika with many daughters.
And ten more by you.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 7.11 (SN 7.11, SN 197, PTS [1st ed. SN i 172, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 369) 2.
Upāsakavagga (The Chapter on Lay Followers)
The Kasibhāradvāja Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Ekanālā, a brahmin village, in the region of Dakkhiṇāgiri.
Now at that time, about five hundred ploughs belonging to the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja were being employed at the sowing season.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the place where the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja was working.
At that time, the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja’s distribution of food was in progress.
Then the Blessed One approached the place where the food was being distributed; having approached, he stood to one side.
The brahmin Kasībhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing for alms, and seeing him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“I, ascetic, plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat. You too, ascetic, should plow and sow; having plowed and sown, you should eat.
“I too, brahmin, plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat.”
“We do not see, Master Gotama, a pair of oxen, nor a plough, nor a ploughshare, nor a goad, nor bullocks; yet Master Gotama says:
‘Brahmin, I too plough and I sow, and having ploughed and sown, I eat.
Then the brahmin Kasī-Bhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“You claim to be a farmer,
yet I do not see your plowing;
being asked, O farmer, tell me.”
"How may we know you for certain?
"Faith is the seed, austerity the rain,
and wisdom is my yoke and plough."
Moral shame is the pole, moral dread the crossbar, the mind is the yoke-tie,
and mindfulness is my ploughshare and goad.
Guarded in body and guarded in speech, I am one who dwells with restraint.
Restrained in food and in my belly,
I practice truth as my sleep;
gentleness is my liberation.
Energy is my yoke-bearing ox,
carrying me toward security from bondage;
it moves forward without turning back.
Wherever one goes, one does not grieve.
Thus is this plowing accomplished;
it has the Deathless as its fruit.
“Having plowed this furrow,
one is liberated from all suffering.
“May the venerable Gotama eat.”
“You must be a farmer, sir,
for you, Master Gotama, practice the plowing that has the deathless as its fruit.
“What is sung to the accompaniment of verses is not fit to be eaten by me.”
This is not the Dhamma for those who see clearly, O Brahmin;
the Buddhas reject verses sung as a chant.
When the Dhamma exists, O Brahmin, this is the proper way of life.
And with food and drink, attend upon the Great Sage who is complete, whose taints are exhausted, and whose remorse is stilled.
"For that field indeed belongs to one who seeks merit.
When this was said, the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Master Gotama! ... [as before] ..."
“From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, I go for refuge.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 7.12 (Upāsakavagga)
The Udaya Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the brahmin Udaya.
Then the brahmin Udaya filled the Blessed One’s bowl with rice.
A second time, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the brahmin Udaya...
[as before] ...And a third time, the brahmin Udaya, having filled the Blessed One’s bowl with rice, said this to the Blessed One:
“This ascetic Gotama is coming again and again; he is very persistent.
“Again and again they sow the seed;
again and again the King of the Gods sends down rain.”
Again and again the farmers plow the field;
again and again the country yields grain.
Again and again the beggars beg.
Again and again the givers of gifts give;
having given again and again, the givers of gifts go to the heavenly realm.
Again and again the milkers milk her;
again and again the calf approaches its mother;
again and again she grows weary and quivers.
The fool enters the womb again and again;
he is born again and again, and dies again and again,
and again and again they carry him to the cemetery.
“Having attained the path to the state of no further becoming,
the one of vast wisdom is not born again and again.
When this was said, the brahmin Udaya addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as above] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.13* (SN 7.13, SN 199, PTS [1st ed. SN i 174; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 375)
2. The Chapter on Lay Followers (Upāsakavagga).
The Discourse on Devahita.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was afflicted by a wind ailment,
and the Venerable Upavāṇa was his attendant.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Upavāṇa:
“Come now, Upavāṇa, find some hot water for me.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Upavāṇa replied to the Blessed One.
Having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, he went to the residence of the brahmin Devahita. Upon arrival, he stood to one side in silence.
The brahmin Devahita saw the Venerable Upavāṇa standing silently to one side.
Having seen him, he addressed the Venerable Upavāṇa in verse:
“You stand there, sir, in silence;”
"Shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe,
what do you desire, what do you seek,
and for what purpose have you come to beg?"
“The Arahant, the Sugata in the world,
the Sage, is afflicted by wind;
if there is warm water, [bring it].”
Give to the sage, O brahmin.
Honored among those worthy of honor, he is the one who should be honored among those worthy of respect.
"I desire that he who is worthy of honor be honored.
Then the brahmin Devahita had a man take a carrying-pole of hot water and a bundle of molasses, and gave them to the Venerable Upavaṇa.
Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bathed the Blessed One with warm water and, having stirred molasses with warm water, gave it to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One’s affliction subsided.
Then the brahmin Devahita approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the brahmin Devahita addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Where should one give a gift?”
Where is a gift given of great fruit?
How indeed does one who sacrifices succeed,
and how is an offering fulfilled?”
“He who knows his former abodes,
sees heaven and states of woe,
and has reached the destruction of birth— ”
The sage who has reached the culmination of direct knowledge—
here one should give a gift worthy of being given;
here what is given bears great fruit.
"In this way, for the sacrificer, the sacrificial gift succeeds.
When this was said, the brahmin Devahita said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 7.14 (SN 7.14, SN 200, PTS [1st ed. SN i 175, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 377)
2. Upāsakavagga Mahāsālasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Then a certain wealthy brahmin, shabby and clad in shabby robes, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As that wealthy brahmin was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Why, brahmin, are you so shabby and clad in such shabby robes?"
“Master Gotama, here I have four sons.
They are driving me out of the house, having consulted with their wives.
“In that case, brahmin, having mastered these verses, speak them in the assembly when the great crowd has gathered and your sons are seated together:”
“Those by whose birth I would rejoice,
and for whose sake I would desire existence—
let them consult with me regarding my wives.”
They are driving away the pig.
Indeed, those wicked people,
my dear, address me as "Father, Father."
Rākṣasas take the form of sons and abandon one who has reached old age;
like a worn-out horse, he is useless.
Food is being taken away;
the elder, who is the father of children,
begs for alms at the houses of others.
A staff indeed is better for me than disobedient sons;
it restrains even a fierce ox.
And likewise, even a fierce dog,
when it is in the dark,
finds a footing in deep water.
“By the power of the staff,
one who has stumbled stands up again.
Then that wealthy brahmin, having mastered these verses in the presence of the Blessed One, spoke them in the assembly when the great crowd had gathered and his sons were seated together:
“Those by whose birth I would rejoice,
and those for whose sake I would desire existence—
let them consult with me regarding my wife.”
They are warding off the boar.
Indeed, those wicked wretches call out to me, "Father!
Father! as if I were their own.
Rākṣasas take the form of sons and abandon one who has reached old age;
like a worn-out horse, he is useless.
Food is being taken away;
the elder, who is the father of children,
begs for alms at the houses of others.
A staff indeed is better for me than disobedient sons;
it restrains even a fierce ox.
And likewise, even a fierce dog,
when it is in the dark of the city,
finds firm footing in the deep.
"By the power of the staff,
he who has stumbled stands up again.
Then his sons led that wealthy brahmin back home, bathed him, and each presented him with a pair of garments.
Then that wealthy brahmin, taking a pair of garments, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wealthy brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, we brahmins indeed seek a teacher’s fee for our teacher.”
"May Master Gotama accept from me this teacher's fee.
Out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted it.
Then that wealthy brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
2. Upāsakavagga:
Mānatthaddhasutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a brahmin named Mānatthaddha was residing in Sāvatthī.
He did not pay homage to his mother, nor did he pay homage to his father, nor did he pay homage to his teacher, nor did he pay homage to his elder brother.
At that time, the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, surrounded by a great assembly.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Mānatthaddha:
"This ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a great assembly.
What if I were to approach the ascetic Gotama?"
“If the ascetic Gotama addresses me, I too will address him;
if the ascetic Gotama does not address me, I too will not address him.
Then the brahmin Mānatthaddha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood silently to one side.
But the Blessed One did not speak to him.
Then the brahmin Mānatthaddha thought,
"This ascetic Gotama knows nothing at all," and he wished to turn back right there.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the brahmin Mānatthaddha, addressed the brahmin Mānatthaddha in verse:
“Pride is not good, O brahmin;
for one who has need of it here, O brahmin,”
“Whatever purpose he came for,
let him fulfill that very thing.
Then the brahmin Mānatthaddha [thought]:
“‘The ascetic Gotama knows my mind!’—thinking thus, she fell right there at the Blessed One’s feet with her head, kissed his feet with her mouth, stroked them with her hands, and announced her name:
‘I am stiff with pride, Master Gotama! I am stiff with pride, Master Gotama!
Then that assembly was struck with a sense of wonder.”
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
For this brahmin Mānatthaddha neither bows down to his mother, nor bows down to his father, nor bows down to his teacher, nor bows down to his elder brother;
yet he performs such supreme acts of reverence toward the ascetic Gotama.”
Then the Blessed One said this to the brahmin Mānatthaddha:
“Enough, brahmin! Arise and sit on your own seat, since your mind has gained confidence in me.”
Then the brahmin Mānatthaddha, sitting on his own seat, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Toward whom should one not harbor pride?
Toward whom should one have respect?”
“Who would be honored?
Who, when well-worshipped, would be truly propitiated?
“The mother and the father.”
Furthermore, toward an elder brother,
a teacher, and a fourth [relative],
one should not harbor pride toward them.
Toward them he should be respectful,
and they should show him honor;
it is good that they are well-honored by him.
To the Arhats who have become cooled, who have done what was to be done and are free from taints—
having struck down conceit, one who is not deluded,
“...those who are unsurpassed, you should revere them.
When this was said, the brahmin Mānatthaddha said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! ... [as before] ...”
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.16 (SN 7.16, SN 202, PTS [1st ed. SN i 179, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 385) 2. Upāsakavagga*
The Discourse on Opposition.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a brahmin named Paccanīkasāta was living in Sāvatthī.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Paccanīkasāta:
"What if I were to approach the ascetic Gotama?
Whatever the ascetic Gotama says, I shall contradict every single word of it."
Now at that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth in the open air.
Then a brahmin who delighted in opposition approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One as he was walking:
"Speak, ascetic, on the duty of a recluse!"
“By one who is bitter in opposition,
well-spoken words are not easily understood;
by one whose mind is defiled, [they are likewise not understood].”
And by one who is full of aggression.
But he who, having subdued aggression and the lack of confidence in the mind;
“Having relinquished resentment,
he indeed would know what is well-spoken.
When this was said, the brahmin Paccanīkasāta said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
2. Upāsakavagga, Navakammikasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, the brahmin Navakammika-Bhāradvāja was having building work carried out in that forest grove.
The brahmin Navakammika-Bhāradvāja saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain sal tree, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
“I find delight in having work performed here in this forest grove.
What does this ascetic Gotama find delight in having performed?
Then the brahmin Navakammika Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“What work is being done by you,
monk, in this sāla grove,
that you are alone in the forest?”
“Gotama finds delight.
[The Buddha replied: “I have no need for a forest;
the forest, with its beautiful sights, has been cut off at the root by me.”
“Svāhā! I am extinguished in the forest, free from the arrow;
alone, having abandoned discontent, I delight.
When this was said, the brahmin Navakammika Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as above] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.

2. Upāsakavagga Kaṭṭhahārasutta On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in a certain forest grove.
Now at that time, several young brahmin students of the Kaṭṭhahāraka clan, who were pupils of a certain brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan,
approached a certain grove. Having approached, they saw the Blessed One sitting in that grove,
having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Having established [the offerings], and having seen [him], they approached the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan;
having approached, they said this to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan:
"Please, sir, you should know."
“In such-and-such a grove a recluse is seated, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, together with those young students, approached that grove.
There he saw the Blessed One seated in that grove, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Having plunged into the empty forest, a wilderness devoid of people, in a deep and very terrifying grove;”
O Bhikkhu, you meditate with a beautiful form, standing motionless and graceful;
where there is neither song nor instrumental music— there you dwell.
A sage dwelling alone in the forest, amidst the woods—
this appears to me as something truly wonderful,
that he dwells in the forest with a joyful heart all by himself.
I imagine that you, desiring the unsurpassed triple heaven and fellowship with the Lord of the World,
have taken up residence in this lonely forest. Why is this?
“You are performing austerity here for the sake of attaining the state of a Brahmā.
“Whatever doubts or attachments there may be,
which are always settled upon the many diverse elements;”
All longings, which arise from the root of ignorance,
have been brought to an end by me, along with their roots.
Thus, I am free from doubt, independent, and unattached.
With vision purified regarding all phenomena,
having attained unsurpassed and auspicious full enlightenment,
I meditate alone in seclusion, O Brahmā, confident and fearless.
When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … From today forth, for as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to him.”

The Discourse to the Beggar.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then a brahmin beggar approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Bhikkhaka said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, I am a mendicant, and you too are a mendicant; what, then, is the distinction between us here?
“It is not by that alone that one is a mendicant.”
To the extent that one begs from others and adopts the conduct of a layperson,
one does not thereby become a bhikkhu.
The one who, having abandoned both merit and evil,
lives the holy life and wanders through the world with discernment—
“He indeed is called a bhikkhu.
When this was said, the brahmin Bhikkhaka said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! … [as above] …”
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.

The Saṅgārava Sutta.
The setting was Sāvatthī.

Now at that time, a brahmin named Saṅgārava was living in Sāvatthī; he was one who sought purification through water, believing that purity comes through water, and he spent his days and nights devoted to the practice of descending into water.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal, on his return from the almsround, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, here in Sāvatthī there lives a brahmin named Saṅgārava who is a purifier by water; he believes in purification by water and dwells devoted to the practice of bathing in water morning and evening.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would go to the residence of the brahmin Saṅgārava out of compassion.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the brahmin Saṅgārava; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As the brahmin Saṅgārava was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Is it true, brahmin, that you are a purifier by water, that you seek purity through water, and that you dwell devoted to the practice of descending into water morning and evening?
"It is so, Master Gotama."
“But what benefit do you perceive, brahmin, that you regard purification by water as true purification, and that you dwell devoted to the practice of bathing in water morning and evening?

“In this case, Master Gotama, whatever evil deed I have done during the day, I wash away with my bath in the evening; whatever evil deed I have done during the night, I wash away with my bath in the morning.”
“Seeing this purpose, Master Gotama, I am a purifier by water; I profess purification by water, and I dwell devoted to the practice of bathing in water morning and evening.
“The Dhamma is a lake, brahmin, with virtue as its bathing place;
it is undisturbed, praised by the virtuous, and lauded by the good.”
"Where indeed those who possess perfect knowledge, having bathed,
cross over to the further shore as if their limbs were not wet.
When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
2. Upāsakavagga Khomadussa Sutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Khomadussa.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered the town of Khomadussa for alms.
Now at that time, the brahmin householders of Khomadussa had gathered in the assembly hall for some business, and the rain was falling drop by drop.
Then the Blessed One approached that assembly hall.
The brahmin householders of Khomadussa saw the Blessed One coming from afar,
and upon seeing him, they said this:
“What are these shaveling ascetics, and who will understand the true nature of the assembly?
Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin householders of Khomadussa with a verse:
“That is no assembly where the virtuous are not present.”
“Those who do not speak of the Dhamma are not holy;
having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
those who speak the Dhamma are indeed holy.”
When this was said, the brahmin householders of Khomadussa said to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost..."
Or one might show the way, or one might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been clarified by Master Gotama in many ways.
We go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The second chapter on lay followers is concluded.
Its summary verse:
Kasi Udaya, Devahita,
and Aññatara Mahāsāla;
Mānatthaddha and Paccanīka—
The novice, the wood-gatherer,
the one who supported his mother, the alms-seeker,
and Saṅgārava with the linen cloth— these twelve.
The Connected Discourses on Brahmins is complete.
